article.overview: An antenna measurement system is an instrument or test arrangement used to characterise a radio antenna: how strongly it radiates or receives in each direction (its radiation pattern), how much gain it provides, and how it performs across frequency. In the lunar context the term could mean a ground-test facility used before launch, an in-space or surface measurement of an antenna's performance, or an instrument that measures the radio environment that antennas must work in. The catalogue entry does not specify which, so this article covers all three readings and treats the verified examples as context rather than as the payload itself. No flown, flight-qualified or publicly described lunar payload carrying this exact name was identified in this research. The Lunar Pathfinder S-band antenna shown below is a candidate antenna under test rather than a measurement system; it is included because it is the only lunar-communications antenna in this research with a verified direct image.
article.description: An antenna's performance is defined by several linked properties: its radiation pattern, gain (the concentration of power in preferred directions compared with an ideal reference), polarisation, impedance and frequency response. Measuring these properties normally requires a controlled environment. On the ground, engineers use anechoic chambers or near-field scanning ranges, in which a probe samples the field close to the antenna and the far-field pattern is computed from those samples. NASA's Horizontal Planar Near-Field Facility is an example of this kind of ground infrastructure. A NASA AMTA 2025 conference paper describes it as a spaceborne antenna test facility with a 10 m by 10 m scanner covering 1 to 110 GHz, and notes that it can drive large vehicles for in-situ upper-hemisphere measurements, citing lunar vehicles as an example. This source was read only through a search summary because the full PDF exceeded the retrieval size limit, so these figures should be confirmed against the paper itself. Measurement on the Moon is far harder. The antenna's surroundings, including the lander structure and the regolith, change the pattern that is actually observed. A February 2026 arXiv preprint modelled a horizontal dipole above a dielectric half-space as a stand-in for regolith and found that coupling to the ground reduces skyward gain, over 1 to 50 MHz and heights of 0 to 5 m. The preprint notes that the dielectric properties of lunar regolith are still largely unknown, especially on the far side. This is a simulation, not a measurement. Historical lunar-mission material points to the same problem from a different angle. A JPL technical memorandum lists a section on gain measurements of the Advanced Antenna System using Surveyor I signals. Only its table of contents was available, so the method and results could not be confirmed.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purposes of an antenna measurement system depend on the reading adopted. Ground verification confirms that an antenna meets its specified pattern, gain and frequency performance before a mission; this is established practice, but the lunar-mission examples in this research are limited to the facility described above. In-situ verification measures the performance of a deployed antenna in its real installation, including ground-plane and structural effects. An ISS-based NASA SCAN Testbed study is described in a search summary as a template for lunar in-situ work, because it captured real ground-plane and blockage effects that simulation can miss; this was not read in full and is a proposed approach. Environment measurement characterises the radio environment that surface antennas will encounter; the ROLSES instrument flown on IM-1 is an example of this purpose. Applications for lunar communication and navigation include validating link budgets for surface-to-orbit and surface-to-surface communication, and checking the performance of relay and navigation antennas. These applications are proposed uses, not demonstrated results from a named lunar system.
article.operating_principle: Two general approaches are used. In an active measurement, a reference source of known power and known position transmits, and a receiver measures the received amplitude and phase as the geometry changes; the measured pattern is compared with the expected one. Near-field methods sample the field close to the antenna and transform it to a far-field pattern. These are standard antenna-measurement principles; the lunar-specific sources used here do not describe a full procedure. In a passive measurement, the instrument records the ambient radio and plasma-wave environment without transmitting. ROLSES is a passive example: it digitises the signal from its antennas, processes it onboard using a fast Fourier transform, and also sends raw waveforms to Earth, which helps the study of dust impacts. ROLSES measures the environment with its own antennas; it does not measure the radiation pattern of a separate antenna.
article.scientific_importance: Knowledge of how antennas and radio signals behave on the lunar surface matters for communications and navigation infrastructure. ROLSES was designed to characterise the radio and plasma-wave environment of the lunar nearside across 2 kHz to 30 MHz, and its stated aims include the lunar plasma sheath and radio emissions from the Sun, the Milky Way and the Earth. Measurements of this kind inform both science and the design of future surface antennas. The lack of published lunar-surface antenna-pattern measurements, identified in this research, is itself an important scientific and engineering gap.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an antenna measurement system. A ground test facility, an in-space gain measurement and a surface radio receiver differ in mass, size, power and interfaces. The examples below are not directly comparable and should not be read as variants of one design.

examples.name: ROLSES (Radio-wave Observations at the Lunar Surface of the photoElectron Sheath)
examples.type: Flown lunar radio and plasma-wave instrument (not an antenna-pattern measurement system)
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Intuitive Machines IM-1 lander, Odysseus. The lander landed tilted near the lunar south pole. The arXiv abstract reports initial observations during transit and on the surface despite the tilted landing. A secondary report gives a combined operating time of about 20 minutes; this is not confirmed by the primary paper and is treated as unresolved.
examples.antenna_mounting_heights: Four antennas mounted at two different heights; the heights are not stated in the source text consulted.
examples.frequency_range_note: 2 kHz to 30 MHz according to the arXiv abstract. A NASA-linked slide deck and a later ROLSES-1 paper give different lower limits (2 kHz and 5 kHz respectively) in search summaries; the primary paper is used here.
examples.digitisation: Each antenna signal is digitised to 14 bits at 120 million samples per second, with an onboard FFT.
examples.deployment: Antennas stowed for launch and deployed after landing using a frangibolt mechanism.

examples.name: Lunar Pathfinder S-band antenna and antenna pointing mechanism (SANT)
examples.type: Proposed lunar communications antenna in development (not a measurement system)
examples.flight_status: SSTL reports functional testing at its Guildford laboratory and expected launch towards the end of 2025. That date comes from a February 2024 article and could not be checked against a later source; current launch status is unverified.
examples.pointing_mechanism: Swashplate-based antenna pointing mechanism (APM) reaching up to 25 degrees off-centre
examples.mission_role: Part of the primary payload of the Lunar Pathfinder spacecraft, for communicating with assets on the lunar surface and in lunar orbit.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The dimensions of a generic antenna measurement system cannot be stated. The ROLSES antennas are 2.5 m monopoles; the overall instrument envelope is not stated in the source consulted. The SANT reflector is 0.86 m in diameter; its total mechanical envelope is not stated in the source consulted.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The mass of a generic antenna measurement system cannot be stated. For ROLSES, mass is not stated in the sources consulted (null). For the SANT, SSTL gives the APM mass as 9.3 kg, or 11.3 kg with the antenna installed; the total payload mass is not stated.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not stated for ROLSES or the SANT in the sources consulted. No power value is given for a generic antenna measurement system.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar surface antenna must withstand extreme temperature cycling, vacuum, radiation and dust. The ROLSES abstract explicitly links its raw waveform data to the study of dust impacts, which shows that dust is an operational consideration as well as a measurement target. Antenna performance also depends on the local ground. A regolith with unknown dielectric properties can change the pattern of a low antenna through capacitive coupling. The lander structure may block or reflect signals, which is why in-situ measurement captures effects that a ground test cannot. A mechanism that must point an antenna, such as the SANT APM, requires a stable reference and suitable thermal and structural design; the source gives its range of motion but not its accuracy or environmental qualification.
article.limitations: No publicly described lunar payload with this exact name was identified, so any article on the payload necessarily treats the name as a functional class. The term 'antenna measurement system' can refer to a ground facility, a surface antenna test or a radio environment instrument; these are not interchangeable. The ROLSES instrument measures the radio environment, not a separate antenna's pattern. The NASA facility figures come from a search summary, not the full paper. The regolith-coupling result is a simulation, and regolith dielectric properties remain largely unknown. The Surveyor gain-measurement study was seen only as a table of contents.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Surface payload considerations apply to ROLSES, which was carried to the Moon on a commercial lander and deployed after landing. The SANT is not a surface payload in its current role; it is part of a spacecraft's primary payload, so its transportation is that of the spacecraft. No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified for any antenna measurement system in this research.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument or antenna into a spacecraft or lander payload configuration on Earth.
Launch it on a launch vehicle.
Deliver it to the surface with a lander, if it is a surface system.
Deploy and position the antennas, using the mechanism required by the design.
Protect the instrument thermally and mechanically, then connect power and data.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ROLSES antennas were stowed for launch and deployed after landing by a frangibolt mechanism; deployment is therefore a mechanism-dependent step that must be verified for any new design. The SANT deployment method is not described in the source consulted, and it is not a surface payload in its current role.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: ROLSES was carried to the Moon on the IM-1 lander and deployed after landing. The Lunar Pathfinder spacecraft is the carrier for the SANT.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified for any antenna measurement system in this research. The Lunar Pathfinder spacecraft and the IM-1 lander are discussed only as the carriers of the examples above.

article.historical_significance: Lunar-mission radio work has long relied on antenna and signal measurements. Surveyor radio tracking was used for phase-coherent two-way Doppler, supporting orbit determination. A JPL memorandum on Advanced Antenna System gain measurements using Surveyor I signals is the closest historical lead to an in-space antenna measurement, but its method and results remain unconfirmed in this research. The Apollo S-band communications antenna is described in a 1967 Electronics article as four 31-inch parabolas clustered around a wide-beam horn; this description comes from a search summary and was not read in full. ROLSES is the most recent verified example in this research of a flown instrument that uses antennas to characterise the lunar radio environment.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Identity of the payload: the catalogue name does not identify a specific mission, so every section is conditional on which reading is intended. No lunar surface antenna pattern measurement was found in the searches. The NASA Horizontal Planar Near-Field Facility figures are unverified beyond a search summary. The regolith coupling result is a simulation. The ROLSES primary abstract does not state an operating duration; the secondary 20-minute figure conflicts with the primary's language on initial observations. ROLSES mounting heights, mass and power were not available from the source consulted. The SANT launch date is from a February 2024 article and needs confirmation. The Surveyor gain-measurement method and results are unconfirmed. Only one image was verified (SANT); no ROLSES or NASA image was verified, and reuse rights for the SANT image are not established. Several sources were read only through search summaries.

data_quality_notes: No publicly described lunar payload with the exact name 'Antenna measurement system' was identified. The article treats the name as a functional class and discloses the reading adopted (ground facility, in-situ measurement or radio-environment instrument).
The ROLSES example measures the radio environment with its own monopole antennas; it is not an antenna-pattern measurement system.
ROLSES frequency lower limit differs between sources (2 kHz in the primary arXiv abstract and a NASA-linked slide deck; 5 kHz in a later ROLSES-1 paper summary). The primary abstract value is used.

ROLSES operating duration conflicts: the primary abstract reports initial observations during transit and surface operations without a duration, while a secondary Universe Today report gives about 20 minutes combined. The primary is used; the duration is unresolved.
ROLSES mounting heights, mass and power were not available from the source consulted and are recorded as null.
The NASA Horizontal Planar Near-Field Facility figures (10 m by 10 m scanner; 1 to 110 GHz) are from a search summary because the full PDF exceeded the retrieval size limit and must be confirmed.
The regolith dielectric coupling result (arXiv:2602.22194) is a simulation, not a measurement.
The SANT launch date ('towards the end of 2025') is from a February 2024 article and could not be confirmed against a later source.
The Surveyor I Advanced Antenna System gain-measurement study was seen only as a table of contents; its method and results are unconfirmed.
The Apollo S-band antenna description comes from a 1967 Electronics search summary and was not read in full.
Only one image was verified (the SANT test image, visually checked). No ROLSES or NASA image was verified. Reuse rights for the SANT image are not established.
No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified for any antenna measurement system.
